first_impression.reaction: My daughter sent this with 'Mum, is this right?' because she's deciding whether to take his name. Honestly, it's her paperwork, not mine. But the second paragraph says marrying overseas changes things, and they're talking about overseas, so I'll read it properly. The opening is plain and calm, no gushing, which I appreciate.

journey.quote: A name change after marriage in Australia is a choice, and it does not happen on its own: you update each record yourself.
journey.reaction: Good. Straight to the point, and it doesn't lecture her either way about whether she should change it.

journey.quote: Marry overseas and the picture shifts.
journey.reaction: That's the line that made me keep reading. Nobody had mentioned this to us.

journey.section: Step 1: Get the official registry marriage certificate (not the ceremonial one)
journey.quote: The handsome certificate you sign at the ceremony is a keepsake.
journey.reaction: I didn't know that, and I've been married thirty-odd years. I'd have assumed the one you sign on the day is the real thing. Useful.

journey.section: Step 1: Get the official registry marriage certificate (not the ceremonial one)
journey.quote: Ask your celebrant early whether they will order it.
journey.reaction: Practical. A clear thing she can actually do, not just information.

journey.section: Step 2: Update your photo ID first (driver licence)
journey.quote: In NSW, take your official marriage certificate and current driver licence to a Service NSW centre.
journey.reaction: We're in Melbourne. NSW gets the step-by-step and Victoria gets 'check with your state's transport agency'. I'd have liked a line for us too.

journey.section: Changing your name on your passport after marriage
journey.quote: It recommends booking travel in the name that's in your passport.
journey.reaction: This is the one I'll send back to her. If we're helping pay for the honeymoon flights, I don't want them turned away at the airport over a name. Clear and sensible.

journey.section: State by state: NSW, Victoria, Queensland and Western Australia
journey.quote: As at November 2026, the registries agree on the broad shape but word the details differently.
journey.reaction: I read Victoria carefully because that's us, but then Queensland and Western Australia say much the same thing again. I started skimming here.

journey.section: Name change after an overseas or destination wedding
journey.quote: An overseas marriage is generally recognised at home, but you cannot register an overseas marriage at home, so there is no Australian marriage certificate to use.
journey.reaction: Now this matters to us. Explained plainly, and it reassures me the marriage itself still counts. I'll forward that to my husband.

journey.section: Name change after an overseas or destination wedding
journey.quote: Victoria says the same application is needed, while Queensland and Western Australia say some organisations may need a formal change of name, as set out state by state above.
journey.reaction: I had to read this twice. Is it 'needed' or 'may need'? For us in Victoria I take it as needed, but it's a tangle of states in one sentence.

journey.section: Name change after an overseas or destination wedding
journey.quote: Bring home the certificate issued where you married, and read how to get your overseas marriage certificate before you leave.
journey.reaction: Then three links in a row: the certificate, the translation, the apostille. It's thorough, but it feels like a reading list for my daughter to work through on her own.

journey.section: Name change after an overseas or destination wedding
journey.quote: One Wedded Advisor, start to finish, plans the venue, travel, vendors and payments as your single point of contact; the name change and every certificate stay with you and the official agencies.
journey.reaction: One named person, start to finish, and they're honest about what they don't do. I'd rather that than someone promising to handle the government side and then not.

journey.quote: One Wedded Advisor plans the venue, travel, vendors and payments with you, anywhere in the world, with the fee agreed in writing before any work begins.
journey.reaction: Fee in writing before any work begins. That's what my husband will look for.

unanswered_questions: If they marry overseas, will the Wedded Advisor at least remind them to collect the official local certificate before they fly home, even if the name change itself is theirs to do?
What does Victoria's transport agency actually need to change the name on a licence?
Is the first step a phone call with a real person before anything is booked or paid?

turn_offs_found.quote: Victoria says the same application is needed, while Queensland and Western Australia say some organisations may need a formal change of name, as set out state by state above.
turn_offs_found.why: This is the section that matters most to a family planning a destination wedding, and this sentence piles three states and two different rules into one line. On the iPad I lost track of which applied to us. One plain sentence per state, or just 'see your state above', would be easier.

turn_offs_found.quote: In other states, check with your state's transport agency for its process and documents.
turn_offs_found.why: The detailed steps are written for NSW, and the rest of us get told to go and find out ourselves. As a Victorian reader it makes the article feel like it wasn't written with us in mind.

would_share_with: My daughter, with 'It recommends booking travel in the name that's in your passport.' and the keepsake certificate point
My husband, with the overseas paragraph ('there is no Australian marriage certificate to use') and 'with the fee agreed in writing before any work begins'

cta_reaction.quote: Start the conversation with Wedded Concierge.
cta_reaction.why: The paragraph before it says the right things: one Advisor, fee agreed in writing. But this article is about my daughter's surname, not the wedding, so I wouldn't enquire off the back of it. If she and I were already looking at planners, this would nudge me towards a call, and I'd want to speak to someone before anything is booked.

top_3_changes: Untangle 'Victoria says the same application is needed, while Queensland and Western Australia say some organisations may need...' into a plain line per state, or simply point back to the state section.
In Step 2, add a line for Victoria (and ideally Queensland) alongside the NSW Service NSW detail, rather than only 'check with your state's transport agency'.
In the overseas section, turn the three back-to-back links into a short 'before you fly home' checklist (collect the certificate, translation, apostille) so it reads like a plan rather than homework.

checks.check: Every journey point, turn-off and CTA reaction has an exact quote from the draft
Stayed in character as Margaret (mother of the bride, Melbourne, paying about half, sent the link by her daughter, reads top to bottom on an iPad)
No invented brand facts; missing details listed as unanswered questions
HTML comments, image slots and VERIFY markers treated as invisible
Deferred business details and transfers not raised as must-fix; absent prices or fee amounts and sourcing not raised as problems, per orchestrator
Journey types limited to the allowed enum; every turn-off has a why

open_questions.question: Relevance is naturally low for a parent on a name-change topic; trust and tone are strong. Main gaps: a tangled multi-state sentence in the overseas section, NSW-only licence detail (Victorian reader), and a link-heavy 'bring the certificate home' paragraph that could be a checklist. Call-first is a deferred business detail.

assumptions: Margaret's daughter is considering a destination wedding and taking her partner's surname; they live in Victoria. Margaret reads the whole article on an iPad.
Fee amounts are deliberately absent and the brand does not discuss sourcing, so neither was raised.
